newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: FEATURE-U.S. surgeons give Colombians a smile.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-U.S. surgeons give Colombians a smile.

text.p: Hundreds of children from poor Colombian families crossed the country by mule, bus and foot this month in search of a smile and the promise of a new life.

They and their families -- drawn by radio and TV advertisements beamed into shantytowns and impoverished rural zones -- went in search of a group of medical Pied Pipers, most from the United States. Many braved the roadblocks set up by leftwing guerrillas that are paralysing almost half the country or sacrificed the last pesos from their monthly budgets to get to one of four hospitals in different regions.

The 132-strong team of doctors and nurses flew to Colombia in the first week of September and set to work repairing young faces disfigured by genetic deformities or burns. The mission, part of an international programme called "Operation Smile," included five days of dawn-to-dusk surgery from Sept. 9-13 during which more than 550 youngsters were treated.

"In the space of just five days, hundreds of children will have been given new lives after being hidden in shame. In this day and age and at a time when the United States and Colombian governments are fighting, this is an opportunity to show that problems can be solved by people who have compassion and understanding for each other," programme founder Dr. Bill Magee from Norfolk, Virginia, said.
"Operation Smile is not a political or a religious organisation but we do tap into the best of people's spirits," he said of the group started in 1982 that has done charity work around the globe.

For his first day of operations at San Ignacio hospital, a well-equipped private facility in Bogota, Magee picked out a particularly tricky case -- 14-year-old Solangel Zamora, from Cundinamarca province just north of the capital. The boy had not been able to talk properly or eat anything but fluids since his jaw fused shut when he was five.

In a painstaking three-hour operation, Magee cut open his teenage patient's scalp, took muscle tissue from his temple region and used it to make a new jaw. The hole in Zamora's temple was then filled with a special plastic.

Magee's colleagues also went to work in three other hospitals in the provincial cities of Cali, Manizales and Duitama. Their donation of their time was matched by thousands of dollars in cash and material sponsorship -- 90 percent from multinational companies operating in Colombia. The total cost of the mission, one week screening patients and one week operating, was about $1 million.

Mother-of-seven Maria Luisa Navia Burbano brought her son Hugo, 9, from their home in Ciudad Bolivar, a working-class area on the edge of the capital. "If it wasn't for Operation Smile I'd be banging on doors asking the neighbours and family for money. We were born poor but we try to feed our children and improve their lot -- I thank the American people for the help they're giving us. These doctors have come to do real social work in the name of the underpriveleged," she said.

Hugo, until now the butt of cruel jokes by his peers because of his cleft lip, put on a brave face as he looked forward to the day he can grin like the rest of the children in the schoolyard. He, like some of the other patients, will need a follow-up operation but this will likely be performed by Colombian surgeons thanks to the lessons learned from their U.S. counterparts.

"I saw an advertisement on TV for Operation Smile on Friday and that very day I said I would take Luis to Bogota," said Adelmo Gomez, a coffee farmer from Cundinamarca province whose son has a cleft lip and palate. "Children tease my son but I always tell him not to take any notice. He's brave and he trusts me that everything will work out fine."

When the flying medics head back to their operating rooms in the United States, the guerrilla war will still be raging in Colombia's countryside and cities and the political crisis sparked by allegations that President Ernesto Samper took drug money for his election campaign looked set to continue.
But at least some of Colombia's new generation have been given something to smile about.
